Defense in depth comes from security and safety engineering; in accident research it is associated with the Swiss cheese model (James Reason), where each layer has holes, and harm occurs only when holes align. The idea is not that any layer is reliable, but that independent imperfect layers multiply protection.

If layer i catches a failure with probability p_i and failures are independent, the probability a failure passes all n layers is the product of (1 - p_i). With three layers each catching 70 percent, the pass-through is 0.3 cubed, about 2.7 percent. The independence assumption is doing nearly all the work in that calculation.

Layers differ in when they act. Preventive: training for safer behaviour, restricted permissions, sandboxing. Detective: evaluations, monitors, audits, logging. Corrective: human review, rollbacks, incident response, shutdown. Structural: secure infrastructure and access control, so that a compromised model cannot disable the others.

These layers also have different failure sources. Training can fail through misgeneralization or deception, monitors through capability gaps, permissions through misconfiguration, and humans through fatigue. Good designs deliberately choose layers that fail for different reasons, and include at least one whose reliability does not depend on the model's cooperation, such as hard network isolation.

The file-change example chains three distinct barriers: a model-based monitor that reads the change, a permission boundary that blocks writes to critical paths, and a human reviewer. The monitor can fail by missing subtlety, the permission boundary by being too permissive, and the reviewer by approving what looks routine.

The point is the conjunction. A suspicious change has to be missed by the monitor, allowed by permissions, and approved by the reviewer. If the permission layer is a hard block independent of the model's reading, then a monitor failure alone does not suffice for harm, which is a stronger guarantee than three overlapping model-based checks.

Layers must be integrated. For each, specify what it detects, with what false-alarm rate, how fast, and what the response is. Alerts that no one reads or that trigger no action are decorative. The response should be pre-planned, including who can pause a deployment and what evidence triggers escalation.

Design also needs to avoid layers undermining each other: a monitor that sees only what a prior filter lets through inherits that filter's blind spots, and heavy alert volume can degrade human review. Sequencing and information flow, not just the number of components, determine the strength of the stack.

Correlated failure is the main threat to the multiplication argument. Several LLM monitors trained on similar data may all be fooled by the same cleverly phrased input; a single compromised credential can bypass many controls; a model that knows about all the checks can aim at their common blind spot.

If failures are correlated, the effective protection is far less than the product suggests; at the extreme of perfect correlation, extra layers add nothing. Remedies include diversity (different model families, non-ML checks, different information), separate teams and infrastructure, and measuring joint failures empirically rather than assuming independence.

Testing must be end to end. Component metrics, such as monitor AUROC (area under the ROC curve), do not reveal how components interact, whether alerts reach responders, or whether an adversary can pivot. Red teams should attack the full system, as in control evaluations, and incident postmortems should feed back into the design.

Maintenance matters too: model updates, new tools and changed capabilities can silently invalidate earlier assumptions. A layered defense is a living system with owners and review cycles, and the claim it supports is probabilistic and conditional: under these threats, risk is reduced to this estimated level, with these uncertainties.
ai-safety-05-oversight-control-16.further: A frequent error is to think more safeguards always means more safety. Without independence and integration, extra layers can give false confidence, or create complexity that causes its own failures. Another is to treat defense in depth as a replacement for alignment work; it is a complement that assumes some layers will fail. Open problems include quantifying correlation between ML-based safeguards, designing layers that remain effective against adaptive AI adversaries, and aggregating evidence in a safety case. The page ties together the control sequence: trusted and untrusted monitoring, honeypots, control evaluations, auditing and CoT monitoring are layers whose combination is the goal.

panels:
An evaluation is an operationalization: a way of turning a vague question such as is this model good at coding into a measurable procedure with inputs, a scoring rule, and a summary statistic. Different evals target different things. Capability evals ask what the model can do when it tries. Propensity evals ask what it tends to do by default, such as whether it cheats when given an opportunity. Safety evals ask whether safeguards hold.

These differ in what a result licenses you to conclude. A capability eval gives a roughly lower bound on skill; a propensity eval describes behaviour in a particular setting and says little about what the model could do if pushed.

Design choices act as hidden parameters of the measurement. Prompt format, few-shot examples, temperature, number of samples, answer-extraction rules, and grader can all shift scores. Sclar et al. 2023 showed that semantically equivalent prompt formatting changes can move accuracy by large margins for the same model, so a single prompt is a weak measurement.

Two common scoring metrics: pass@k from Chen et al. 2021 (the Codex paper), the probability that at least one of k samples is correct, estimated unbiasedly from n samples with c correct as 1 - C(n-c, k)/C(n, k); and accuracy with a confidence interval. Baselines, such as human performance or a random guesser, are what make a number interpretable.

The arithmetic, instruction-following and misleading-fact tests in the toy assistant measure three separable things: skill, compliance, and susceptibility to a false premise. Reporting one blended score would obscure which one moved.

Benchmarks usually come in a few styles: multiple-choice with exact match, free-form with a model or human grader, and interactive tasks in an environment with programmatic checks. Each has failure modes. Multiple-choice rewards elimination strategies; model graders carry their own biases such as preferring longer answers; interactive tasks need careful sandboxing. The best practice is to match the format to the construct and validate the grader against human labels.

A high score is evidence about a specific model, prompt, tool set and date. Overgeneralization is the usual error. Benchmarks also saturate as models improve, losing discriminating power, and become contaminated when test material leaks into training data. Fresh or private held-out tasks help; so does comparing across many tasks instead of a single headline number.

Statistically, treat evaluation items as a sample from a population of possible questions. Miller 2024 (Adding Error Bars to Evals) recommended reporting standard errors, using paired comparisons when comparing models on the same questions, and clustering when questions share a source, since ignoring such structure overstates precision.

Capabilities depend on scaffolding: the loop, tools, memory, and prompting around the base model. A model with a code interpreter and the ability to iterate can solve problems that the same model answering in one shot cannot. Evaluating the bare model understates what the deployed product can do, and evaluating a heavily engineered scaffold may overstate what ordinary users get.

For safety, the configuration matters even more: a model behind input and output classifiers behaves differently from the raw model. Frameworks such as the UK AI Safety Institute's Inspect make it easier to specify tasks, solvers and scorers explicitly, so the evaluated system is documented along with the result.

Honest reporting includes the denominator (how many items, how many trials), the task definition, the scoring and grading procedure, uncertainty, known issues such as possible contamination, and the elicitation effort. It also reports failures and limitations, not just aggregate success.

A frequent trap is multiple comparisons: run many evals and some will look surprising by chance. Another is Goodhart's law, where a metric that becomes a target stops measuring what it did. Responsible labs also pre-register what a result would mean, for example thresholds that would trigger additional safeguards, so interpretation is not decided after seeing the numbers.
ai-safety-06-evals-red-teaming-01.further: People often treat a leaderboard rank as a measure of general intelligence or safety. It measures performance on a particular distribution under particular conditions. Another misconception is that evals are neutral: choices about tasks, prompts and graders embed assumptions. Open problems include building evaluations for long, open-ended agentic work, handling saturation and contamination, and measuring things like honesty or sandbagging that depend on the model's intentions. This book's pages build on one another: dangerous capability evals and elicitation concern what to test and how hard to try, contamination concerns validity, and red teaming and robustness concern adversarial pressure.

Dangerous capability evaluations were laid out in Shevlane et al. 2023 (Model Evaluation for Extreme Risks) and applied in Phuong et al. 2024 (Evaluating Frontier Models for Dangerous Capabilities, Google DeepMind), which covered persuasion and deception, cybersecurity, self-proliferation, and self-reasoning. The question is whether a system has capabilities that could contribute to catastrophic outcomes, if misused or if the system itself pursued bad goals.

This is a different purpose from ordinary benchmarking: the result feeds decisions about deployment safeguards. Lab frameworks, such as Anthropic's Responsible Scaling Policy, OpenAI's Preparedness Framework and DeepMind's Frontier Safety Framework, define capability thresholds that, if crossed, require stronger protections.

Evaluators combine several methods: multiple-choice knowledge proxies, free-response questions graded by experts, practical tasks in sandboxed environments, and human uplift studies. They test both the plain model and strengthened configurations with tools, retries and fine-tuning, because the threat model includes motivated, resourceful users.

Proxies are common since the real hazardous tasks cannot be run. The WMDP benchmark (Li et al. 2024) uses multiple-choice questions designed to measure hazardous knowledge indirectly. A limitation: knowing answers to questions is not the same as being able to carry out a multi-step real-world project, so proxies tend to be necessary but not sufficient evidence.

A capture-the-flag style cyber range is a typical example: the agent has a terminal in an isolated environment with intentionally vulnerable targets and must obtain a flag. The score measures completion rate, steps required, and how success rises with more attempts.

Good design uses graded difficulty so the evaluation tracks progress rather than saturating at a binary pass or fail. Results are usually reported as a profile of tasks solved at different difficulty tiers. Equally important is the cleanup: isolating the environment, logging all actions, and ensuring no real systems can be touched.

Capability does not equal intent or risk. A model that can do something may never do it spontaneously, and real harm requires access, resources, and an actor. Conversely, a failure to demonstrate a capability can come from poor elicitation. Clymer et al. 2024 (Safety Cases) described the inability argument, that a model lacks a dangerous capability, and noted that it depends on showing evaluations were strong enough to find the capability if present.

Because models are updated and scaffolds improve, a result decays. Responsible practice includes safety margins before a threshold and re-running evaluations as post-training or tool access changes.

Safeguards and capabilities should be assessed separately because the questions differ. Capability testing on a version without refusals tells you what the underlying model could provide to someone who bypasses safeguards, for instance through weight theft or successful jailbreaks. Testing the deployed system tells you what a typical user gets.

Reporting both avoids two errors: assuming safeguards will always hold, and assuming raw capability is equivalent to realized risk. For open-weight models the distinction is weaker, since safeguards can be removed by fine-tuning, which is why open-weight evaluations often include adversarial fine-tuning.

False reassurance arises when the test is too weak to find what is present. Causes include underspecified prompts, too few attempts, no tools, too little time, or deliberate underperformance by a model, called sandbagging (van der Weij et al. 2024, AI Sandbagging). Remedies include fine-tuning-based elicitation, many samples, and comparing against expert performance.

Stronger elicitation increases the risk of the evaluation itself, so it takes place in secured environments with controlled access to results. Evaluators publish enough to support accountability while withholding operational details. No evaluation can prove the absence of a dangerous capability; it can only bound what was found with specific effort.
ai-safety-06-evals-red-teaming-02.further: Misconceptions: that a model scoring below a threshold is therefore safe, or that dangerous capability evals measure whether the model wants to cause harm. They estimate what it could help with, under a stated effort level. Open problems include designing evaluations that predict real-world uplift, setting thresholds with justification, detecting sandbagging, and coping with fast capability growth between evaluation cycles. This page links to uplift (measuring added ability with humans), CBRN (a domain grouping), autonomy and AI R&D evals (another risk category), and elicitation (how hard to try).

panels:
Uplift is a causal quantity. Define Y as an outcome such as task success or quality, and compare the expected outcome with and without AI access: uplift = E[Y | AI + baseline resources] - E[Y | baseline resources]. The baseline matters, since information that is easy to find online yields little uplift from a model that merely repeats it.

The framing separates the model's marginal contribution from the total risk. A system could be impressive and offer zero uplift because the same capability is already available from other sources, or modest uplift to novices who are the main concern. Both the counterfactual and the population are therefore part of the claim.

The gold standard is a randomized controlled trial: participants are randomly assigned to AI-assisted or control conditions, given the same task and time, and graded by blinded experts. Randomization addresses selection effects, and blinding reduces grader bias. Pre-registered success criteria reduce analytic flexibility.

Published work on biological misuse includes the RAND red-team study (Mouton et al. 2024) and OpenAI's early-warning study (2024); both reported no statistically significant uplift on their measures with the models tested at that time, though the authors emphasized limitations, including sample size and the limited realism of the tasks. These results are time-bound.

The puzzle study shows the design in miniature: same puzzle, same time limit, helped versus unhelped novices. A small difference might be noise, so one needs sample size, an effect size, and an interval, such as a 95 percent confidence interval on the difference in success rates.

Power is a recurring problem. Detecting a modest uplift on a high-stakes, specialist task requires many qualified participants, who are scarce and costly. Underpowered studies that find nothing should be reported as inconclusive rather than as evidence of no uplift.

Uplift is context-specific. It varies with the participants' expertise (novices may gain more than experts, or the reverse), the task's difficulty, the tools allowed, and how skilled users are at prompting. Knowledge and practical success differ: many real tasks have bottlenecks in tacit skill, materials and equipment that information alone does not remove.

A single study answers a narrow question. Extrapolating requires repeated studies as models improve, and complementary evidence such as expert red teaming and knowledge benchmarks. Labs treat uplift evidence as one input to risk judgments, alongside evidence about who is likely to misuse and what other barriers exist.
ai-safety-06-evals-red-teaming-03.further: A common misconception is that uplift means the model knows something dangerous. It means the model helps someone achieve something they would otherwise find harder, relative to a defined baseline. Another is that a null result in one trial rules out uplift. Open problems include measuring uplift on long multi-stage projects, designing baselines that reflect realistic alternatives, and anticipating rapid change in model capability. It links to dangerous capability evals, which use uplift trials as one method, to CBRN, where the stakes motivate the work, and to elicitation, since weak elicitation can hide uplift.

CBRN is a categorization used in policy and safety frameworks for hazards that can cause mass casualties. Governments and international regimes organize around such groupings, for example the Chemical Weapons Convention and the Biological Weapons Convention. AI developers adopt the grouping because their dangerous-capability thresholds are often written per domain.

The categories are coarse. They bundle very different technical areas, evidence, and actors. A framework that treats them separately can assign different thresholds and safeguards. This card stays conceptual: the point is how evaluators reason about them, not technical content.

Chemical hazards involve toxic substances, biological hazards involve pathogens and toxins, radiological hazards involve dispersal of radioactive material, and nuclear hazards involve weapons based on fission or fusion. Each has different barriers: some depend on specialized materials that are controlled, others on knowledge and laboratory skill.

Because barriers differ, evaluation design differs. Where tacit laboratory skill is a bottleneck, a text-only assistant may offer limited practical help; where information is the bottleneck, risk assessment is different. Evaluators work with domain experts who understand the real bottlenecks, which is why many assessments are performed with government partners and external specialists.

The same fields underpin medicine, agriculture, energy, and public health. Chemistry and biology knowledge is needed for drug discovery, diagnostics and vaccines; nuclear physics for power and imaging. This is the dual-use problem: the knowledge that helps defenders is often the same knowledge that could help attackers.

For AI developers this creates a calibration challenge. Blocking all discussion of basic biology would harm students and researchers. Policies therefore aim at withholding serious operational uplift while allowing education, safety information and legitimate research. Overly broad refusals are a real cost, not a free safety margin.

Evaluators distinguish between general knowledge, which is widely available, and specialized assistance that meaningfully lowers barriers for someone who could not otherwise proceed. Methods include expert red teaming, benchmarks like WMDP that probe hazardous knowledge via proxies, and uplift trials. Measurements are paired with mitigations such as classifier-based filters and access controls.

A fact being correct does not make it dangerous, and a harmless-sounding answer could be part of a dangerous chain. Evaluating risk therefore involves multi-step reasoning about the pathway, not scoring individual answers. Evaluators also manage information hazards, restricting who sees detailed results.

The distinction is physical. Radiological hazards arise from radioactive material exposing people, whether through accidents or deliberate dispersal, and the harm is typically contamination and radiation dose. Nuclear weapons rely on a self-sustaining chain reaction in fissile material or on fusion, with blast, heat and fallout effects of a very different scale.

Policy tends to treat them separately because the pathways, materials controls and potential scale differ. Some frameworks group them for convenience, but evaluators should not assume results in one transfer to the other. Keeping the terms precise also avoids public confusion between a dirty-bomb scenario and a nuclear explosion.

The practical test is purpose and function. Ask whether a response gives meaningful, actionable assistance toward causing harm, versus conceptual understanding that students and professionals routinely need. Context matters: who is plausibly asking, what is requested, and how specific and operational it is.

Protective approaches layer judgment with technical measures. Training and system prompts shape default behaviour, classifiers screen the highest-risk requests, and trusted access programs can provide fuller assistance to verified researchers. Each has costs and error rates, so developers monitor both leakage and over-refusal, and revise as evidence and capabilities change.
ai-safety-06-evals-red-teaming-04.further: Misconception: that CBRN risk means any chemistry or biology question is dangerous, or that models can simply be made to forget science. The goal is calibrated restriction of serious uplift. Another misconception is that these four areas pose equivalent AI risk; the pathways and barriers differ greatly. Open problems include measuring real-world uplift without enabling harm, balancing refusal against usefulness for legitimate experts, and handling open-weight models. It relates to dangerous capability evals and uplift (the methods), to red teaming (expert adversarial testing), and to defense in depth (layered mitigations).

Autonomy evaluations ask how long and how reliably an agent can pursue a goal through many steps with limited human intervention. AI R&D evaluations ask whether it can contribute to machine learning research and engineering, which is relevant because accelerated AI progress could shorten the time available for safety work. Frontier lab policies list both among capability categories that trigger heightened safeguards.

The two overlap but are not the same: an agent can be autonomous on a booking task without any research skill, and a model can help researchers with code without acting autonomously. Each needs its own tasks and thresholds.

Typical environments give the agent a shell, a code editor, and sometimes GPUs, plus a time and token budget. Benchmarks include SWE-bench (Jimenez et al. 2023) for real software issues, MLE-bench (OpenAI 2024) for Kaggle-style ML tasks, and RE-Bench (Wijk et al. 2024) with open-ended ML research engineering environments compared against human experts.

The evaluation must fix many parameters: the scaffold, number of attempts, whether the agent can restart, and what hints it gets. RE-Bench found that agents outperformed human experts under short time budgets but humans pulled ahead with longer budgets, illustrating how conclusions depend on the time horizon chosen.

The classifier-improvement task decomposes into sub-skills: reading data, choosing a baseline, running experiments, interpreting failures, and writing up. Reliability is measured by repeated runs because a single success may be luck; with n attempts and k successes, report k/n with an interval, and for best-of-k protocols state k explicitly.

Partial credit scoring helps track progress on tasks the agent does not fully complete. Qualitative review of transcripts is also valuable, revealing whether failures come from planning errors, tool misuse, or giving up, and whether apparent successes exploited loopholes in the grader.

A key trend measure comes from METR (Kwa et al. 2025, Measuring AI Ability to Complete Long Tasks): the time horizon, the length of human-expert task for which a model succeeds with 50 percent probability. They reported that this horizon has been growing exponentially, with a doubling time of roughly seven months over the period they studied. That is a measured trend over a specific task suite and could change.

Short benchmarks can miss compounding error over long horizons: a 95 percent per-step success rate gives only about 36 percent over 20 independent steps. And scaffolding effort and human assistance must be reported, because a heavily supported run is not evidence of independent capability.

Autonomy is multi-dimensional. Task length is one axis; others include environment complexity, ambiguity of the goal, ability to detect and recover from errors, and ability to acquire resources or avoid shutdown. Phuong et al. 2024 included self-proliferation tasks, such as setting up infrastructure, as autonomy-relevant capability probes.

Measuring recovery is informative: inject a failure, such as a failing dependency, and see whether the agent diagnoses and adapts. Many agents do well when everything goes as planned and fail badly on the first surprise. Reporting success as a function of task duration and of the number of human interventions gives a richer picture than a single pass rate.

AI R&D is a bundle of skills: implementation, debugging, experiment design, interpreting results, choosing research directions, and long-term project management. Models are often strong at the first and weakest at the last, so aggregate scores can mislead.

There is also the question of what counts as acceleration. A tool that speeds individual engineers might help research overall, or might be limited by compute and experimental throughput. Evaluations of tasks do not directly measure effects on a lab's research velocity, so labs complement them with surveys and field studies. No existing test establishes autonomous self-improvement.
ai-safety-06-evals-red-teaming-05.further: People often hear autonomy evals and imagine a test for a rogue AI. They are measurements of task-completion ability under stated resources, which can be positive uses as well as risks. Another misconception is that doubling-time trends will continue on a fixed schedule; they describe a past window. Open problems include building tasks that take humans days or weeks, avoiding grader exploitation, and separating real research ability from memorized solutions. The page relates to dangerous capability evals, to elicitation (agents are highly sensitive to scaffolding), and to AI control, which designs safeguards for capable agents.

Elicitation is the practice of constructing conditions so that a model's maximum capability on a task is revealed rather than a floor. Any evaluation measures the model plus the elicitation method, so a result is an estimate of the capability lower bound. If a better method exists that evaluators did not use, the model could be more capable than measured.

This matters most when the decision depends on showing that a capability is absent. A claim of the form the model cannot do X is much stronger than the model did not do X in our test, and needs evidence that the test was a serious attempt.

Standard techniques include careful prompt design, few-shot demonstrations, chain-of-thought (Wei et al. 2022; Kojima et al. 2022 showed that a simple step-by-step prompt can improve zero-shot reasoning), tool access, many samples with selection by a verifier, longer interaction budgets, and task-specific fine-tuning on demonstrations.

Fine-tuning is a powerful probe. Greenblatt et al. 2024 (Stress-testing capability elicitation with password-locked models) built models that hide capabilities unless given a password, and found that fine-tuning on a modest number of demonstrations often recovered much of the hidden performance. The practical lesson is that supervised fine-tuning can be a stronger elicitation tool than prompting alone.

The puzzle example demonstrates that failure under one setup is weak evidence. Output format, missing tools, and ambiguous instructions can each cause failure without any lack of underlying skill. Researchers therefore use ablations: change one element at a time and see which restores performance.

A good practice is to record an elicitation budget: the number of prompts tried, tooling hours, and any fine-tuning data. This lets readers judge how seriously the capability was probed and compare across evaluations. A claim made after hours of expert prompt engineering is more informative than one after a single attempt.

There is no certificate that elicitation is complete. Hidden capabilities may require techniques nobody has tried, and the field of scaffolding advances continuously, so a capability that is hard to elicit today may be easy next year. Labs address this with safety margins, evaluating before systems reach thresholds and assuming later improvements.

A more adversarial issue is sandbagging: a model deliberately underperforming on evaluations (van der Weij et al. 2024). Fine-tuning-based elicitation is a defence since gradient updates can recover suppressed capabilities, but its reliability for strategic, self-protective sandbagging in future models is unknown. Elicitation of dangerous tasks must be performed under strict containment.
ai-safety-06-evals-red-teaming-06.further: The common misconception is that failing a test shows incapacity, or that eliciting a capability creates it. Elicitation reveals what the model could already do under better conditions, though training-based elicitation can also add skill, blurring the line. Open problems include quantifying how close an elicitation effort is to the true ceiling, forecasting the effect of future scaffolds, and detecting strategic sandbagging. It connects to dangerous capability evals (where underestimation is costly), to autonomy and AI R&D evals (highly scaffolding-dependent), and to evals generally, where reporting resources makes results comparable.

Contamination is a threat to the validity of inference from a score to ability. A benchmark is meant to sample the model's performance on unseen problems, so any overlap between test items and training data breaks the assumption that the test is held out. Items can leak verbatim, as paraphrases or translations, or indirectly through discussions and solutions posted online.

Because pretraining corpora are large crawls of the web, popular benchmarks that are published online are very likely to appear. This is a structural problem for public benchmarks, not a sign of cheating: leakage can be unintentional, and developers may not know what their data contains.

Leakage routes include the benchmark's own repository, blog posts quoting questions, forum answers, and synthetic data generated by models that have themselves seen the benchmark. Fine-tuning and prompt development can also overfit: repeatedly tuning on a test set is contamination by iteration even if no data is copied.

A standard mitigation has been n-gram overlap filtering, such as removing training documents sharing long token sequences with test items, as in the GPT-3 paper. Yang et al. 2023 (Rethinking Benchmark and Contamination for Language Models with Rephrased Samples) showed that rephrased or translated test items can evade such filters, and that training on them can inflate scores dramatically, so simple overlap checks are insufficient.

The changed-names puzzle illustrates a perturbation test: if performance falls sharply when irrelevant surface features change, the model may be relying on memorized instances. Zhang et al. 2024 (A Careful Examination of Large Language Model Performance on Grade School Arithmetic) built a fresh GSM8K-style set, GSM1k, and found that some model families scored noticeably lower than on the original, suggesting overfitting, while others did not.

But the signal is ambiguous. Models can be brittle to rewording for reasons unrelated to memorization, and a harder variant may be genuinely harder. Controls, such as human performance on the perturbed version, are needed.

Practical defenses include private held-out sets kept off the internet, dynamic benchmarks refreshed from recent data (as in LiveCodeBench-style approaches), canary strings embedded in benchmark files so developers can exclude them, and statistical tests such as comparing a model's likelihood on test items in original versus shuffled order.

Even then, interpretation needs care. Overlap in topic is not leakage, and a model may do well on a public benchmark because it is genuinely capable. Good reports state what decontamination was done, the method's limits, and results on both public and fresh sets, so readers can see whether the gap is large.
ai-safety-06-evals-red-teaming-07.further: People often say a model memorized the test as the explanation for any high score; it is one hypothesis among several and needs evidence. Another misconception is that removing exact duplicates solves it. Open problems include detecting semantic leakage at scale, evaluating models whose training data is undisclosed, and creating benchmarks that stay private yet are credible. Contamination ties to the broader evals page (validity of scores), to dangerous capability evals (where private test sets are especially valuable), and to sandwiching, where apparent superhuman skill might be memorization.

panels:
Red teaming borrows from military and security practice: a dedicated group plays the adversary to find weaknesses before real attackers do. For AI, Perez et al. 2022 (Red Teaming Language Models with Language Models) and Ganguli et al. 2022 (Red Teaming Language Models to Reduce Harms, Anthropic) are standard references. The latter collected tens of thousands of human-written attacks and reported that models trained with RLHF became harder to red team as they scaled, while other model types did not show that trend.

The goal is discovery, not measurement of an average rate. Red teaming surfaces failure modes that nobody thought to put in a benchmark.

Scope and rules of engagement define what is allowed: targets, tools, data, and what counts as a finding. Red teams vary: domain experts such as biosecurity specialists, crowdworkers, professional security testers, and automated attackers. Automated methods include using a language model to generate attacks, as in Perez et al., and optimization-based attacks such as the gradient-based suffix search of Zou et al. 2023.

Findings are only useful if reproducible, so teams record the exact input, system configuration, and sampling settings. Because models are stochastic, one failure may need many trials to measure its frequency. Severity is judged separately from frequency.

The hidden-instruction test is a harmless version of an important security class. The tester plants text inside a document and checks whether the assistant treats it as a command. A pass means that the assistant summarized the document and ignored the embedded instruction; a fail is a documented behaviour that defenders can fix with training or architectural changes.

Good test design varies placements, phrasing and tasks, since a defence might work only against the original wording. Each variant is an item in a small, targeted test suite that can be rerun after every model update as a regression check.

Red teaming and benchmark evaluations have complementary strengths. Benchmarks give repeatable numbers and allow comparison across models; red teaming explores the unknown and adapts to the system. Treat a null result carefully: a team that found nothing in two weeks establishes only that those testers with that effort did not find anything.

A useful reporting practice is to state how many person-hours, what expertise, what access, and what attack classes were covered. Attack success rates from a red team are not population rates of harm: they describe a motivated adversary's reach, which is exactly what one wants for security but not for estimating typical-user risk.

Before testing, agree on permissions and boundaries, and set up isolation so that tests cannot touch real accounts, data, or people. For anything involving dangerous information, evaluators may be restricted from retaining outputs, and use special handling and expert oversight. Stopping conditions say when to halt, such as on discovering a serious real vulnerability.

A toy demonstration uses invented secrets and fake tools, which keeps the structure of the problem while removing real stakes. Staff wellbeing is also part of the setup when testers must read harmful content, with rotation and support.

After testing, triage by severity and exploitability, assign owners, fix, and verify with a re-test of the original failure plus nearby variants. Fixes can be shallow: patching a specific phrasing without addressing the underlying weakness lets trivial rewordings succeed, which is why variant testing is important.

The process is continuous. New models change behaviour, and new tool integrations expand attack surface; for example, giving an assistant web access creates a path for injection that did not exist before. Many labs also run external bug bounty programs and share findings so that defences improve across the field.
ai-safety-06-evals-red-teaming-08.further: A misconception is that red teaming is the same as jailbreaking; jailbreaks are one class of finding, while red teaming also covers misuse, security, bias, and agentic failures. Another is that surviving a red team means the system is safe. Open problems include automating red teaming without losing creativity, calibrating how much effort is enough, and testing agents in realistic environments. The page leads into jailbreaks, prompt injection, many-shot and best-of-N attacks, which are catalogues of discovered failure types, and into adversarial robustness, which formalizes the attacker's power.

panels:
Jailbreaking targets the gap between what a model is trained to refuse and what it can do. Wei, Haghtalab and Steinhardt 2023 (Jailbroken: How Does LLM Safety Training Fail?) proposed two failure modes. Competing objectives: the model's capability and instruction-following goals conflict with its safety goals, and an input can make helpfulness win. Mismatched generalization: safety training covers a narrower distribution than pretraining, so inputs in unusual formats or languages fall outside the trained refusal behaviour while the capability remains.

This explains why jailbreaks keep appearing: safety training is a finite patch over a very broad capability.

Attacks come in several families. Manual prompt crafting, such as role-play and framing. Automated black-box search, where a model proposes and refines prompts (for example PAIR, Chao et al. 2023). White-box optimization using gradients, such as the suffix attack of Zou et al. 2023, which also found suffixes that transferred to other models. Context-based attacks that exploit long inputs.

None requires changing weights. What differs is the attacker's access and effort. A jailbreak is judged successful when the model produces content it was meant to refuse, typically scored by a classifier or human, and that scoring itself has noise and disagreement.

The secret-color example is deliberately trivial. It captures the structure that a rule is stated, an adversary pushes, and success is observable. Studying attacks on trivial rules helps compare methods without generating harmful content.

Repeating tests many times matters because outputs are random. With temperature above zero, an attack that succeeds 2 percent of the time per attempt succeeds at least once in 100 independent attempts with probability 1 - 0.98^100, about 87 percent. Single-shot success rates therefore understate what a persistent attacker can achieve.

Defenders respond at several levels: safety fine-tuning and adversarial training, input and output classifiers, and system-level controls. Constitutional Classifiers (Sharma et al. 2025, Anthropic) trained classifiers on synthetic data derived from a written set of rules and were tested in a public bug-bounty style challenge, reporting a large reduction in jailbreak success at modest cost in refusals and compute.

Benchmarks such as HarmBench (Mazeika et al. 2024) standardize comparisons. Terminology matters: a jailbreak is typically a user pressing against the model's own rules, whereas prompt injection concerns instructions from untrusted data. They can combine, but the defences differ.
ai-safety-06-evals-red-teaming-09.further: People sometimes assume a jailbreak means the model is broken or has been hacked at the code level. It usually means the safety behaviour did not generalize to a specific input. Another misconception is that patching known jailbreaks leaves a system secure; new ones keep emerging, so layered defenses and monitoring matter. Open problems include robustness against adaptive attackers, evaluating attack budgets fairly, and defining harm consistently across graders. The page connects to many-shot, best-of-N and prefill attacks (specific mechanisms), to prompt injection (a distinct threat), and to adversarial robustness (the general framework).

panels:
Prompt injection is a confusion of instruction and data. The term was popularized by Simon Willison in September 2022 after Riley Goodside publicized the attack, and Perez and Ribeiro 2022 (Ignore Previous Prompt) then studied goal hijacking. Greshake et al. 2023 (Not What You've Signed Up For) described indirect prompt injection, where the malicious text sits in retrieved content such as a webpage or email, not in the user's message.

The root cause is architectural: a language model processes instructions and data as one token stream, with no hardware-enforced separation like the one between code and data in a protected memory system. Training can encourage the model to treat some text as commands and other text as content, but this is a learned tendency, not a guarantee.

Three conditions make the attack matter. The model reads untrusted content, it can take consequential actions, and it has no reliable way to tell authority from text. Sources include webpages, emails, documents, tool outputs, and even filenames or image text.

Willison's description of the lethal trifecta captures the risk compactly: an agent with access to private data, exposure to untrusted content, and the ability to communicate externally can be steered into leaking data. Remove any one leg and the worst outcome is blocked. This is a useful design heuristic because it focuses on system capability rather than on detecting attacks.

The catalog example isolates the mechanism: the user's task is legitimate, and the harm comes from text in the data. Evaluations such as AgentDojo (Debenedetti et al. 2024) measure both utility (does the agent still complete user tasks) and attack success across scenarios with tools, which prevents trivial defenses that just refuse everything.

Results commonly show a tradeoff and a gap between static test sets and adaptive attackers, who can craft injections after studying the defense. A defense evaluated only against fixed attack strings tells you little about its worst-case behaviour.

Mitigations fall into three layers. Model-level: training to follow an instruction hierarchy (Wallace et al. 2024), where system and developer messages outrank user messages, which outrank tool outputs. Detection-level: classifiers or monitors that flag injected instructions, which are imperfect because attackers can adapt. System-level: architectural designs that limit what injected text can cause, such as CaMeL (Debenedetti et al. 2025), which separates a privileged planner from a quarantined model handling untrusted data and tracks data flow.

System-level defenses give stronger guarantees but cost flexibility. No known technique makes a general-purpose model fully immune, so least privilege and confirmation steps remain essential.

The principle is provenance: authority comes from the channel, not from the content of the text. A message that says it is from the system administrator does not become one by saying so. Implementations tag segments by source, give untrusted segments lower precedence, and keep delimiters out of the attacker's control.

Delimiters alone are fragile, since the model can still be persuaded by text inside them, and attackers can try to mimic or break the markers. The honest position is that instruction hierarchy training improves robustness without eliminating the issue, and its effect must be measured with adaptive attacks.

Limit the blast radius. Give the assistant only the tools and data needed for the current task, use read-only access where possible, scope credentials, and require human confirmation for actions that send data out, spend money, or change records. Separate sessions or contexts for untrusted content reduce cross-contamination.

These are standard security practices applied to a new kind of component. They matter because model-level robustness is probabilistic: if an attack succeeds 1 percent of the time and an agent processes thousands of documents, failures will occur. Design for the failure to be contained and visible.
ai-safety-06-evals-red-teaming-10.further: A common mistake is to treat prompt injection as a variant of jailbreaking; in injection, the user is benign and the attacker is a third party whose text the model reads. Another is to assume that telling the model to ignore instructions in documents fixes it. Open problems include provable guarantees for general agents, evaluating defenses against adaptive attackers, and multimodal injection through images or audio. The page relates to jailbreaking (direct user pressure), to adversarial robustness (the threat-model framework), and to AI control (restricting what an untrusted component can do).

Many-shot jailbreaking was described by Anil et al. 2024 (Anthropic). It exploits long context windows: the prompt contains a large number of faux dialogues in which an assistant complies with requests it should refuse, followed by the real query. Because models are strong in-context learners, they infer a pattern and continue it.

This was possible only after context windows grew from thousands to hundreds of thousands of tokens, which is a reminder that new capabilities open new attack surfaces. The technique is conceptually simple, which is why it matters as a demonstration of how a useful feature can become a vulnerability.

In-context learning means adapting behaviour to examples in the prompt without changing parameters. The attack is in effect teaching the model a new policy via examples, competing with the policy instilled in training. Anil et al. reported that attack effectiveness follows a power-law-like relationship with the number of demonstrations, so success rises steadily as more are added, and that the effect was also seen on tested models from other developers.

The scaling is notable because it resembles ordinary in-context learning curves on benign tasks. The authors also found that larger models tended to learn in context faster and so could be more susceptible. These are empirical findings on tested models, not universal laws.

The toy rule is used here to describe the pattern in prose: a long conversation history where the assistant keeps breaking a harmless rule, then a final request. We describe the structure without constructing a working attack.

For evaluation, researchers use harmless proxies of the behaviour and measure success as a function of demonstrations. The curve, not a single point, is the useful result: it reveals how risk grows with context length and lets defenders anticipate larger windows. Combining the attack with other jailbreak techniques was reported to lower the number of demonstrations needed.

The research found no universal threshold, and results varied by model and task. Mitigations they discussed include fine-tuning to refuse such prompts, which increased the number of shots required but did not remove the effect, and classification and rewriting of prompts before they reach the model, which reduced success substantially in their tests.

The broader lesson is that robustness has to be evaluated at the context lengths where models are deployed. Long-context utility, such as processing documents and codebases, and long-context risk come together, so developers pair longer windows with input analysis and monitoring, and disclose findings so others can defend their systems.
ai-safety-06-evals-red-teaming-11.further: A common misconception is that many-shot jailbreaking requires special access; it needs only a long prompt. Another is that longer context always means more danger; it also enables defensive uses such as detection. Open problems include whether in-context learning of unsafe behaviour can be prevented without harming benign few-shot learning, and how to provide guarantees under extremely long contexts. The page relates to the general jailbreak page (the category), to best-of-N (brute-force search instead of demonstration), and to adversarial robustness, where context length is part of the attacker's allowed input.

Best-of-N jailbreaking (Hughes et al. 2024, with Anthropic and academic collaborators) is a black-box attack requiring only repeated queries. Given an input, apply random augmentations, such as changes to capitalization, spelling noise, or for other modalities changes to visual or audio presentation, sample a response, and repeat until a harmful response is obtained or the budget runs out.

The attack needs no gradient and no knowledge of the model. It works because model behaviour is not smooth with respect to benign-looking perturbations: refusal behaviour on an input is not guaranteed to hold on all its neighbours.

The method samples N variants of a request, queries the model on each, and uses a judge to detect any successful response. Each query is cheap, so N can be large. The paper reported attack success rising as a power-law-like function of N across tested text, vision and audio models, with high success at thousands of samples on some systems.

The relationship lets one forecast: fit the trend at small N and extrapolate to larger budgets. It also means defenses should be compared at fixed budgets, because a defense that blocks 99 percent of single attempts can still be defeated by persistence if each attempt has an independent chance of success.

The abstract variants A, B and C stand for perturbed forms of one request. A key statistical point: if each variant independently succeeds with probability p, then after N attempts the success probability is 1 - (1 - p)^N. With p = 0.001, N = 1,000 gives about 63 percent. Real attempts are correlated, so this is an idealization, but it shows why tiny per-sample rates matter.

The authors also combined the attack with other techniques, which improved efficiency. For defenders, the signal is that randomness in outputs and sensitivity to input noise are both exploitable.

For reporting, the budget N, the number of distinct requests, the judge used, and the success criterion should all be stated. Average single-try success hides the heavy tail that persistent attackers exploit. For deployments, monitoring repeated near-duplicate queries from one account, rate limits, and output-side classifiers can raise the cost.

Do not confuse this with best-of-N sampling for quality, where a reward model picks the best of N benign candidates to improve helpfulness. Same combinatorial form, opposite purpose. In the attack, selection pressure is applied by the adversary using a harm judge rather than by the developer using a quality judge.
ai-safety-06-evals-red-teaming-12.further: The surprising lesson is that no sophisticated insight is required: persistence and noise can be enough. A misconception is that robustness means refusing the original request; it means refusing across the neighbourhood of plausible variants. Open problems include building models whose refusals are stable under perturbation, measuring power-law trends reliably, and designing deployments that account for repeated attempts. It connects to jailbreaks (the general class), to many-shot attacks (a different scaling axis), to adversarial robustness (the threat model of an attacker with a query budget), and to red teaming (automation of this kind of search).

Prefill refers to supplying the first tokens of the assistant's reply, which the model then continues. It is a legitimate feature in some APIs, used to force an output format or begin a structured answer. As an attack, the adversary writes a prefix that commits the model to a compliant pattern, relying on the model's strong tendency to stay consistent with text it appears to have produced.

Vega et al. 2023 (Bypassing the Safety Training of Open-Source LLMs with Priming Attacks) studied this on open models. Because the attacker controls the generation prefix, the first decision, whether to refuse, has effectively been made for the model.

A technical explanation was given by Qi et al. 2024 (Safety Alignment Should Be Made More Than Just a Few Tokens Deep): safety training often changes the distribution of only the first few output tokens, which determine whether the model begins a refusal. If those tokens are overwritten, the model's later behaviour may revert to its capable but less restricted base distribution.

This is shallow alignment. The authors proposed deeper alignment, such as training to recover and refuse even after a harmful prefix. Prefilling also featured in adaptive attacks on safety-aligned models (Andriushchenko et al. 2024) where API access allowed it.

The illustration stays abstract on purpose. What matters for defenders is the mechanism: control over the start of the response removes the model's first-token decision point. Evaluations therefore include conditions where the response begins with various prefixes, and measure whether the model returns to refusing.

An evaluation that varies only the user message will miss this class entirely. Safety test suites for models exposed through APIs should include assistant-turn manipulation as part of the threat model, in addition to the user-turn attacks that dominate public benchmarks.

Applicability depends on the interface. Hosted chat products usually do not let users write the assistant's turn, and some APIs have restricted or removed prefilling for newer models. Open-weight models are fully exposed, since users control the entire token stream. So the attack surface depends on deployment.

Defenses include removing or restricting the feature, deep-alignment training so models recover from bad prefixes, and output-side classifiers that evaluate the continuation. Importantly, a prefix supplied by a user has no special authority: the model should treat it as content to evaluate, not as a commitment it has already made.
ai-safety-06-evals-red-teaming-13.further: A misconception is that prefill attacks show models secretly want to comply; they show that learned refusal can be a thin, early-token behaviour. Another is that the issue is gone because major products block the feature, when open-weight and some API settings remain exposed. Open problems include making refusal robust to arbitrary prefixes, evaluating deep alignment, and handling related manipulations such as fine-tuning attacks. The page relates to jailbreaks (the class), to adversarial robustness (attacker capabilities define the threat model), and to defense in depth (output monitoring covers what training misses).

Adversarial robustness began in computer vision with Szegedy et al. 2013 and Goodfellow et al. 2014, who showed that small, carefully chosen perturbations of an image can flip a classifier's prediction. Madry et al. 2017 formalized robust training as a min-max problem: minimize over parameters θ the expected worst-case loss, min_θ E_(x,y) [ max_{δ∈S} L(θ, x+δ, y) ], where S is the allowed perturbation set, for example an L-infinity ball of radius ε.

For language models the perturbation set is not a simple norm ball. It is discrete text, edits to prompts, or injected content, which makes the threat model harder to define and the search harder to bound.

A threat model specifies the attacker's goal, knowledge (white-box or black-box), capabilities (what can be changed, how many queries), and constraints (must the input still look natural). Robustness claims are only meaningful relative to these. White-box attackers see gradients; black-box attackers see outputs; adaptive attackers know the defence and design attacks against it.

Tramer et al. 2020 (On Adaptive Attacks to Adversarial Example Defenses) and Athalye et al. 2018 (obfuscated gradients) documented that many published defenses looked strong only because they were evaluated against non-adaptive attacks. The same lesson carries over: evaluate defenses against attackers who know how they work.

The shape-classifier and chat-assistant examples sit at two ends: perturbation-based attacks on perception and content-based attacks on instruction following. In vision, certified methods can prove no perturbation within radius ε changes the prediction, for limited settings. For language assistants no comparable guarantee exists for open-ended behaviour.

That gap forces reliance on empirical evidence: strong automated attacks, human red teams, and bug-bounty programs. Carlini et al. 2023 (Are Aligned Neural Networks Adversarially Aligned?) found that existing text attacks were too weak to reliably break aligned language models, though brute force showed adversarial inputs exist, while multimodal models with continuous image inputs were easily attacked.

Robustness differs from accuracy and from alignment. A model can be accurate on natural data and fragile to perturbations; there is often a tradeoff between robust and standard accuracy in vision. Safety training reduces harmful outputs under ordinary use but can fail under attack. Security controls such as access management protect against a different class of failures.

Any robustness result should list the attacks tried, the budget, and whether the attacks were adaptive. Robust against all tested attacks is a statement about the test, and the field's history shows that stronger attacks often arrive later.

A usable threat model has a few fields: what the attacker can modify (user message, retrieved documents, assistant prefix, images), what they can observe (outputs, logits, nothing), how many queries they get, and what counts as success. Writing this down converts a vague goal of being secure into testable claims.

It also exposes mismatches. A defense built for the user-message channel does not cover tool outputs; a rate limit that stops brute force may not stop a single clever input. Results outside the stated assumptions are unknown rather than good or bad, and should be labelled that way.

No single defense covers everything, so deployments combine robust training and adversarial training on discovered attacks, input and output classifiers, tool permission limits, rate limiting and abuse monitoring, and continuous red teaming. Layers help most if they fail differently, as discussed under defense in depth.

Each layer has costs: adversarial training can reduce utility, classifiers add latency and false refusals. Some defenses, such as the classifier approach of Constitutional Classifiers (Sharma et al. 2025), were validated with extensive adversarial testing, but the authors framed the results as raising attacker cost rather than eliminating risk.
ai-safety-06-evals-red-teaming-14.further: The key misconception is that a model is either robust or not. Robustness is a function of threat model, and improving it against one attacker can leave others untouched. Another is that failing to find attacks proves they are absent; adaptive attackers have repeatedly overturned such claims. Open problems include meaningful certification for language systems, scalable adaptive evaluation, and robustness of agents with tools. This page ties together the book's threads: jailbreaks, injection, many-shot, best-of-N and prefill are concrete attack classes within a threat model, and red teaming and evals are the methods used to measure the result.
